Antelope jackrabbit (Lepus alleni) parturition results in neonates with a wet weight at birth of approximately 84.34 grams [Wwb = approximately 84.34 grams], a value estimated from the closely related black-tailed jackrabbit (Lepus californicus) given the scant data available for the species. Following a gestation period of 42 days [tg = 42 days] under a typical core body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C], these precocial young are born fully furred with their eyes open, an adaptation to the arid grasslands and desert scrub of southern Arizona and western Mexico. The relatively modest mass of the newborn offspring, compared to the ultimate adult size, suggests a growth strategy oriented toward rapid post-natal mass gain rather than extended altricial development. Females likely produce between one and five pups per litter [N_R_i = between one and five pups per litter] and, under favorable conditions, may complete up to four litters per year [F_R_i = up to four litters per year], a reproductive rhythm that underscores the species' capacity for population increase during periods of abundant forage.

The initiation of lactation and the subsequent suckling juvenile stage proceed over a defined interval before weaning occurs. Based on data from Lepus californicus, the time since birth at weaning is estimated at 69 days [tx = 69 days] when measured at a body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. During this pre-weaning period, the nursing offspring grow rapidly, and the wet weight at weaning is projected to be around 1300 grams [Wwx = around 1300 grams], representing a substantial increase from the birth mass. This dietary transition from milk to solid vegetation marks a critical point in the life cycle, as the young must develop the digestive efficiency required to process the fibrous desert forage that constitutes the primary diet of adults. The cessation of maternal provisioning coincides with the onset of nutritional independence, after which the juvenile must rely entirely on its own foraging success to meet daily energetic requirements and sustain further growth toward the adult stage.

As adults, Antelope jackrabbits attain a maximum adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, reported between 2.7 and 4.73 kilograms, with a central estimate of 4100 grams [Wwi = 4100 grams]. This considerable size, among the largest of North American hares, provides thermal inertia that buffers against extreme temperature fluctuations in their arid habitat and likely contributes to a relatively low mass-specific metabolic rate. Basal oxygen consumption, representing the resting metabolic rate of a post-absorptive individual at thermoneutrality, has been measured at 1650 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 1650 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. The relationship between this substantial body mass and the corresponding metabolic expenditure aligns with general mammalian allometric expectations, though the species may exhibit subtle metabolic adaptations to the heat and water scarcity characteristic of its Sonoran Desert environment.

Sexual maturation in Lepus alleni occurs well after the juvenile growth phase has concluded. Data from the congeneric Lepus californicus, applied here, suggest that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 1095 days [tp = approximately 1095 days] when the animals are maintained at a core temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. This prolonged period before reproductive maturity reflects the extended duration required to attain the skeletal and muscular development necessary to support the high energetic demands of gestation and lactation. Young males typically achieve full testicular descent and spermatogenesis, while females undergo first ovulation around this chronological milestone. The relatively late onset of breeding, compared to smaller lagomorphs, is consistent with life-history theory predictions for a large-bodied species that invests considerable resources into each offspring and faces lower extrinsic mortality rates once fully grown.

Reported maximum longevity for the Antelope jackrabbit, again inferred from data on Lepus californicus, suggests that individuals can survive for approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] at a body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. This lifespan of about twelve years is notable among hares and is likely facilitated by the species' open-country habitat, which offers a diverse array of escape routes and keen sensory capabilities for predator detection. Population turnover, however, can be rapid, as the high reproductive output with litters of one to five pups and up to four litters annually compensates for mortality due to predation, drought, and disease. Age-related physiological decline in the form of reproductive senescence and diminished locomotor performance gradually increases mortality risk in the oldest segments of the population, typically those beyond eight years of age in wild settings. The interplay between this extended lifespan and the moderate reproductive rate defines the species' place along the slow-fast continuum of mammalian life-history strategies.
